title: Turkey Secures Kirkuk Stake in Iraq Energy Deal, Ozel Launches Yeni Parti as Second-Largest Opposition, Lira Hits All-Time High
subhead: Erdogan and Iraqi PM al-Zaidi signed a landmark energy agreement giving TPAO a 15% stake in the BP-run Kirkuk oilfield, with Iraq offering up to 1M barrels/day — just as the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline agreement expired. Ozel formally launched Yeni Parti with 91 MPs, reshaping the parliamentary opposition. Meanwhile, the lira touched 47.42 against the dollar, a new all-time low.

sections.heading: Turkey-Iraq Energy Deal: Kirkuk Stake and Pipeline Crossroads
sections.body:
President Erdogan hosted Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in Ankara on July 28, announcing what he called a 'historic step' in bilateral energy cooperation. State-owned Turkish Petroleum (TPAO) secured a 15% stake in BP Energy Company of Kirkuk Limited, giving Turkey a direct partnership in one of Iraq's largest oilfields, which contains more than 3 billion barrels of oil equivalent in resources, according to Anadolu Agency.

Erdogan confirmed that al-Zaidi offered to supply Turkey with up to 1 million barrels of oil per day. 'Once we transfer 1 million barrels of oil from our neighbour Iraq, it will meet our needs,' Erdogan said at the joint news conference, as reported by Al Jazeera and AP News.

The deal comes as the 1973 Iraq-Turkiye Crude Oil Pipeline agreement expired on July 27. Rather than renew the old framework, Turkey is pushing for a comprehensive new energy cooperation agreement. Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said Turkey wants full-capacity operation of the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline — which can handle 1.5 million bpd but currently flows at only about 180,000 bpd, according to Asharq Al-Awsat. Iraq has requested a one-year extension of the pipeline deal while negotiations continue, Reuters reported in June.

Five cooperation agreements were signed covering transport, infrastructure, education, industrial property, and youth/sports, TRT World reported. Erdogan also said Turkey is ready to supply Iraq with defense industry products and emphasized the importance of the Development Road Project connecting the Gulf to global markets via Iraq — a route that has gained strategic value since the Strait of Hormuz disruption began in February.
sections.whyItMatters: The Kirkuk stake gives Turkey its first direct equity position in Iraqi oil production, transforming it from a transit country to a producing partner. With Hormuz disrupted, both Ankara and Baghdad see the Kirkuk-Ceyhan corridor as a strategic alternative for Iraqi crude exports — and Turkey as a more reliable transit route than the Gulf. The expired pipeline agreement creates leverage for Turkey to push for full-capacity flows and a long-term framework.

sections.heading: Ozel Launches Yeni Parti, Reshaping Parliamentary Opposition
sections.body:
Ozgur Ozel formally registered Yeni Parti (New Party) with Turkey's Interior Ministry on July 28, after being ousted as CHP chairman by a court ruling in May that annulled the party congress electing him. The Chief Prosecutor of the Supreme Court of Appeals confirmed the party's active status, according to Devdiscourse.

91 lawmakers have joined Yeni Parti from the CHP, making it the second-largest party in the 600-seat parliament behind the AKP's 277 seats, Al Jazeera reported. The rump CHP retains only 44 MPs, dropping from the main opposition to fourth place. Ozel declared the party 'the hope of a new beginning' and pledged to back jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu as the opposition's presidential candidate, saying he 'was not elected by a single political party, but by more than 15 million people.'

Two major polls illustrate the party's potential. A Gundemar Research survey (June 24-27, 2,350 respondents) put Yeni Parti at 34.9% — ahead of the AKP at 30.4% — with the Kilicdaroglu-led CHP at just 4.3%. An AREA Research poll (July 11-15, 2,030 respondents) showed Yeni Parti at 19.4%, the AKP at 34.2%, and the CHP at 11.8%, according to Business Turkey Today and Haberler.

However, the split carries risks for the opposition. MEE analysis notes that while Yeni Parti could surpass the AKP, a divided opposition field — with Yeni Parti, CHP under Kilicdaroglu, and potentially other candidates — may hand Erdogan a first-round victory in 2028. Ankara Mayor Mansur Yavas, who polls at 60.6% favorability in the AREA survey, has reportedly decided to remain within the CHP for now, MEE reported.
sections.whyItMatters: Yeni Parti's launch fundamentally alters the opposition landscape. The CHP is now a shell with 44 seats, while Yeni Parti becomes the main opposition force in parliament. But the split means Erdogan faces two opponents who may not coordinate, and Kilicdaroglu's CHP could siphon enough votes in a presidential race to prevent any single opposition candidate from winning outright.

sections.heading: Lira at Record Low as CBRT Holds Steady
sections.body:
The Turkish lira hit a new all-time low of 47.42 against the US dollar on July 28-29, according to Trading Economics data. The USD/TRY rate stood at 47.39 as of July 29, with the lira down 1.61% over the past month and 16.86% over the past 12 months.

The Central Bank (CBRT) held its benchmark rate at 37% for the fourth consecutive meeting on July 23, as widely expected. Annual inflation eased to 32.11% in June from 32.61% in May, but remains far above the CBRT's target. Analysts cited by Xinhua do not expect a rate cut before October, citing elevated inflation expectations, rising energy costs from the US-Iran conflict, and the lira's structural depreciation pressures.

The lira's slide is being driven by three converging factors, according to InvestingCube analysis: elevated domestic inflation, higher oil prices (Turkey imports nearly all its energy; Brent crude rose above $87/barrel amid the Hormuz disruption), and safe-haven dollar demand driven by geopolitical risk aversion. The CBRT's managed depreciation regime continues, but analysts warn that any sharp escalation in oil prices or the Iran conflict could push the lira past 50.
sections.whyItMatters: The CBRT is stuck between a lira in structural decline and inflation that remains above 32%. With oil prices elevated and the Hormuz situation unresolved, rate cuts are off the table for months — keeping borrowing costs punishing for businesses while the lira continues to grind lower. The Iraq energy deal could eventually help the current account, but that impact is years away.

sections.heading: Akkuyu Unit 1 Reaches Cold Hydraulic Testing Milestone
sections.body:
Rosatom Director General Alexei Likhachev visited the Akkuyu nuclear plant site on July 28, confirming that cold hydraulic tests have begun on Unit 1, World Nuclear News reported. The tests verify the tightness and strength of the reactor system components and establish water chemistry parameters before hot testing and fuel loading.

Likhachev said construction work on Unit 1 is now complete, with 1,930 staff assigned to the unit, more than 40% of whom are Turkish citizens. The cold tests are expected to conclude within weeks, followed by hot tests at temperatures above 260 degrees Celsius, and then nuclear fuel loading. Unit 1 remains targeted to begin supplying electricity to Turkey's grid during 2026.

The four-unit, 4,800 MWe plant in Mersin province is Turkey's first nuclear facility, built under a Russian build-own-operate model. When all four units are complete, Akkuyu is expected to meet about 10% of Turkey's electricity needs.
sections.whyItMatters: Cold hydraulic tests are a definitive commissioning milestone — they confirm the reactor's primary systems are physically intact before any fuel goes in. With construction complete and hot tests imminent, Unit 1 is on track for operation this year, which would make Turkey a nuclear power generator for the first time. That matters both for energy security and for Turkey's stated goal of reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels.

sections.heading: Syria Seizes Hezbollah-Bound Arms on Iraq Border
sections.body:
Syria's Interior Ministry announced on July 16 that security forces seized a large arms shipment on the Syrian-Iraqi border destined for Lebanon's Hezbollah, Al-Monitor reported. The cache included long-range missiles, anti-tank guided missiles, and drones, found in a suspicious vehicle in the border zone.

The seizure is part of a broader pattern under President Ahmed al-Sharaa's government, which has been conducting security operations along the Lebanon and Iraq borders since the fall of Assad in December 2024. Syria has dismantled several Hezbollah-linked cells, including one in May accused of plotting to assassinate senior government figures, and discovered two smuggling tunnels on the Lebanese border in March.

Trump has repeatedly called on Syria to help disarm Hezbollah, suggesting in a Fox News interview that al-Sharaa 'would go in and take care of Hezbollah.' Al-Sharaa has rejected military intervention in Lebanon, insisting Syria seeks economic cooperation with its neighbor.
sections.whyItMatters: The new Syrian government is demonstrating it can disrupt Iran's arms supply routes to Hezbollah — a shift from the Assad era, when Syria was the corridor, not the interdictor. For Turkey, which shares Iraq's northern border and has its own PKK concerns, a Syria that actively blocks Hezbollah smuggling is a regional security partner in the making, aligning with Ankara's 'terror-free region' vision that Erdogan discussed with Iraq's al-Zaidi.

sections.heading: Syria-Turkey Border Dynamics and the PKK Peace Process
sections.body:
Erdogan told al-Zaidi that Turkey remains 'in close dialogue with our Iraqi brothers to ensure that our process of a terror-free Turkiye and our vision of a terror-free region become a reality,' Al Jazeera reported. Turkey maintains approximately 50 bases in northern Iraq with some 5,000 soldiers deployed, according to the same report.

The PKK announced its disarmament in mid-2025 as part of a peace deal with Ankara to end 40 years of conflict. However, Turkey continues to view the group's presence in mountainous northern Iraq as a national security threat, and the parliamentary 'Terror-Free Turkiye' bill — reported by Daily Sabah as mobilizing for passage — represents the legislative dimension of the peace framework Erdogan says will 'soon arrive in parliament,' according to Bianet.

DW's analysis noted that the peace process faces unresolved questions about political rights for Kurdish citizens, the status of PKK fighters, and whether the government will follow through on democratic reforms or use the process primarily to consolidate power.
sections.whyItMatters: The PKK peace process is moving from negotiation to legislation, but the gap between rhetoric and implementation remains wide. Erdogan's discussion of the process alongside Iraq's PM — and Turkey's continued military footprint in northern Iraq — signals that Ankara sees the peace process as both a domestic and regional security instrument.

bottomLine: Turkey took its most significant energy step in decades, acquiring a direct stake in Iraq's Kirkuk oilfield just as the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline framework expired — replacing a transit relationship with an equity partnership that could bring 1M bpd to Turkish refineries. In domestic politics, Ozel's Yeni Parti has instantly become parliament's second-largest bloc with 91 seats, but the opposition's fragmentation between Yeni Parti and a gutted CHP under Kilicdaroglu could make Erdogan's path to another term easier. The lira at 47.42 reflects the compounding pressure of high inflation, expensive oil, and geopolitical risk — the CBRT is holding at 37% with no easing in sight. Akkuyu Unit 1 completed construction and began cold hydraulic testing, bringing Turkey closer to nuclear power generation for the first time. And in Syria, the new government's interdiction of Hezbollah arms shipments signals a genuine shift from Assad-era complicity to active disruption — a development with implications for Turkey's regional security calculus.
